title: ‘South Park’ Creators Apologize for the Years-Long Delay of Their Kendrick Lamar Movie: ‘We Still Believe in the Project’
description: “South Park” co-creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone have released an official apology for delaying their mysterious film collaboration with Kendrick
body:
“South Park” co-creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone have released an official apology for delaying their mysterious film collaboration with Kendrick Lamar.

	“We take full responsibility for the schedule delay of this movie,” Parker and Stone said in a statement to The Ankler. “We apologize to our partners at pgLang and Paramount, and we appreciate their patience. ‘South Park’ and life’s circumstances have gotten in the way, but we still believe in the project.”
	

	Reps for Paramount, Parker and Stone did not immediately respond to Variety’s request for comment.


	The musical comedy movie, operating under the working title “Whitney Springs,” is in production at Paramount, which is also the home of “South Park.” Parker and Stone are working on the project under their Park County banner. Lamar is also producing alongside Dave Free and his pgLang company.

	Early loglines stated that “Whitney Springs” follows a Black man working as a slave reenactor at a living history museum who discovers his white girlfriend’s family once owned his ancestors. The Ankler reported a slight variation on the story. The outlet claims that the film follows the Black slave reenactor as he clashes with the racist mayor of a Midwestern town, who will be played by Parker. Lamar, The Ankler said, has recorded several original songs for the project.

	Parker and Stone debut “South Park” Season 29 on Sept. 16. Seasons 27 and 28 came after a two-year hiatus and shocked audiences with the inclusion of Donald Trump as a major antagonist. The show has continued to troll the president in the off season. Parker and Stone recently changed the name of “South Park” to “South America,” in an apparent jab at Trump for changing the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America.

schema.headline: ‘South Park’ Creators Apologize for the Years-Long Delay of Their Kendrick Lamar Movie: ‘We Still Believe in the Project’

title: ‘Entourage’ Creator Slams ‘God-Awful’ Ad Reuniting Jeremy Piven and Adrian Grenier: A ‘S—ty Imitation’ That ‘Makes Me Puke’
description: “Entourage” creator Doug Ellin has spoken out against an ad reuniting Jeremy Piven and Adrian Grenier, calling it a “cheap, shitty imitation” of his
body:
“Entourage” creator Doug Ellin has spoken out against an ad reuniting Jeremy Piven and Adrian Grenier, calling it a “cheap, shitty imitation” of his beloved HBO comedy.

	While Piven and Grenier are technically playing themselves in the ad — not super agent Ari Gold and movie star Vincent Chase — their performances, dialogue and dynamic are certainly reminiscent of “Entourage.” (Piven snakes his way through a mansion party to find Grenier on a yacht, where he pitches him a new movie role.)
	

	“Many people worked really hard to make our show as good as it was,” Ellin wrote on Instagram. “When I see cheap, shitty imitations that try to pass for what we did it makes me puke.”


	On Wednesday, Variety broke the news of Piven and Grenier’s on-screen reunion, which took place in a three-minute spot for Jake Paul’s gambling app Betr. Ellin said in a video message that he received “400 messages” about the “god-awful commercial,” clarifying that he was not involved in its creation.

	Ellin said he’s not bitter over not being paid for the ad. He simply wishes the writers of “Entourage” would get more credit for the hard work they put into the scripts and character development, only for their work to be distilled into an “embarrassing” emulation of the HBO hit.

	“I watch it and I want to throw up, because I would suffer, along with many other people, over every syllable, every fucking word,” Ellin said. “So I watch this trash, this shit, and go, ‘Ugh, ugh.’ There’s no bitterness. I want everyone to get paid, get rich. Just fucking do your own shit. That’s all.”
	

	Ellin then seemed to take a shot at Piven — who won three Emmys for playing Ari on the series — claiming that the actor distanced himself from “Entourage” in the years following the 2011 series finale and 2015 movie.

	“I not only wrote, we found these people. We cast these people,” Ellin said of forming the “Entourage” ensemble. “I actually had to beg Piven to do the show because he didn’t wanna do it. And he didn’t wanna talk about it afterwards. Like, he wanted to get away from it, because he had so much better shit going on. But now he’s back on it, because he’s getting paid.”

	A representative for Piven did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment.

	Responding to Ellin’s comments, a spokesperson for Betr said in a statement, “We were excited to bring Jeremy and Adrian back together, appearing as themselves. Creating that kind of unexpected cultural moment with two amazing actors was exactly what we wanted for Betr 2.0.”

	The statement continues, “We’re really proud of how the spot came together, and the response has been overwhelmingly positive, generating nearly 10 million organic social views in less than 24 hours. We had a lot of fun making it, they had a lot of fun making it, and people seem to be having a lot of fun watching it. We appreciate Doug watching the ad and helping promote it. Betr 2.0 is available now.”

	On another social media app, X, Ellin continued to lash out against the ad. “I have zero positivity in watching things I busted my ass [off] on for years [be] turned into garbage,” he wrote. “Go create your own shit. And if you need money … Flip burgers. This is trash and theft. Period.”

	Responding to a fan who said he hoped Ellin was behind the ad, the “Entourage” creator fired back: “I think it’s pretty damn obvious I didn’t write it. My god.” And, with apparent sarcasm, Ellin replied to a fan asking for an “Entourage” reboot: “Piven should write and direct. I can’t wait [to] watch.”

	Ellin has often been asked about doing an “Entourage” reboot since the series ended 15 years ago. A proper revival has never been in development, but the cast and (for a while) Ellin have expressed an interest in returning to the world of Vinny Chase. Earlier this month, however, Ellin threw cold water on the possibility, saying on the “Joe Vulpis Podcast” that a reboot or spinoff is unlikely, and “I don’t spend one second thinking about ideas unless somebody’s paying me.”
	

	The closest he got to a revival was a 2022 pilot titled “Ramble On,” a dramedy about established stars looking to reinvent their careers that starred “Entourage” favorites including Kevin Connolly and Kevin Dillon alongside Charlie Sheen. Ellin released the trailer for the project, but it ultimately failed to sell to a distributor.

	Ellin currently hosts the “Victory” podcast with “Entourage” star Kevin Dillon.

schema.headline: ‘Entourage’ Creator Slams ‘God-Awful’ Ad Reuniting Jeremy Piven and Adrian Grenier: A ‘S—ty Imitation’ That ‘Makes Me Puke’

title: Billy Joel Says He Had Brain Surgery After His Diagnosis: ‘Don’t Worry About Me’
description: Billy Joel says he is doing better after brain surgery helped relieve some of the symptoms of normal pressure hydrocephalus, a disorder he was diagn
body:
Billy Joel says he is doing better after brain surgery helped relieve some of the symptoms of normal pressure hydrocephalus, a disorder he was diagnosed with in 2025. On SiriusXM’s Billy Joel channel Wednesday, the singer talked about the surgery he agreed to after noticing “my balance was not good, I had this sensation of rocking on a boat.”

	The 77-year-old musician revealed in May 2025 that he had been diagnosed with normal pressure hydrocephalus, in which cerebrospinal fluid builds up inside the skull and presses on the brain. He canceled several concerts and said he had been told not to perform until he recovered.
	

	Though he returned in January of this year to perform two songs with a tribute band, he said on Sirius that in general his doctors have asked him not to undergo too much stress.


	His neurologist said that since it was possible it could continue to get worse, he recommended that Joel have a shunt implanted in his brain. Joel said on Sirius that although he initially didn’t want to have a hole drilled through his brain, after researching it he realized it could help with balance and help memory. 

	“I don’t want to lose my marbles,” he said. “It’s hard to tell what’s your age and what’s a condition.

	“So they implanted a shunt in my brain and it actually improved things. My memory got better, my balance got a little better, my ability to function was better. I realized that because of my job, which is playing rock and roll music very loud, that it was giving me something like a concussion every time I did a show.”

	“I’m ok. I want people to know, don’t worry about me. I’m still here,” he assured fans on Wednesday.

schema.headline: Billy Joel Says He Had Brain Surgery After His Diagnosis: ‘Don’t Worry About Me’

title: ‘The Fire Within You’ Review: An Insufferable Christmas Eve Family Drama in Which the Corrosive Rants Are as Noxious as the Dyspeptic Images

body:
Let’s hope there was a giant extractor fan on the set of “The Fire Within You,” because the stench of burnt oil must have been overwhelming. It’s not only food that gets blistered in Edoardo De Angelis’ overwrought screaming match, which makes one envious of the wax Odysseus had handy to plug up his sailors’ ears. In his case, the sounds were of sirens, whereas the characters here would give the harpies a run for their money, making them seem almost dulcet-toned in comparison. Set in a family’s apartment on Christmas Eve and featuring a mother so monstrous not even the Ancient Greeks could have conjured her up, one can only imagine what kind of pressure was on the Venice Film Festival to place it in competition.
	

	“La mamma è sempre la mamma” is a common Italian expression — “the mother is always the mother” — and her sacred position in the nation’s psyche, tied of course to a couple of millennia spent worshiping the Virgin Mary, renders her an inviolable figure. No matter how nasty she may be, no matter how unfit she is to be a mother, her position is untouchable. For Italian audiences, that means Angela (Vanessa Scalera) can spew bile nonstop, but there’s no question her children will stick by her. For most everyone else, it’s impossible to escape the thought that if they’ve put up with this termagant for so many years, they deserve every moment together. But why drag us into it?


	Angela’s clearly already had a tipple in the kitchen when she excoriates her adult son Antonio (Lino Musella) for not having the guts to slit a live capon’s throat. With a cigarette dangling from her lips, ashes and curse words ever ready to fall, Angela lurches around the house critical of everything and everyone. She pours venom on Antonio, a successful literary editor, telling him he’s a useless wimp. Her daughter-in-law Benedetta (Elena Radonicich) is dismissed for not knowing her way around a stove top and, what’s worse, she’s the reason why Neapolitan-raised Antonio lives in Milan. Grandson Andrea (Samuele Mazza) is a “faggot” because he takes ballet classes, and granddaughter Valentina (Nicole Malaj) is a vegetarian, which makes her pathetic.
	

	Her cooking is as poisonous as her words, yet both gush out in a non-stop flow of over-fried eggplant, aggressively hacked cod and salad drowning in oil. With the arrival of Angela’s daughter Paola (Ivana Lotito), the nastiness increases — at least Paola has the ability to talk back, unlike Antonio, who keeps taking abuse, such as “it would have been better if you had died at birth,” until he finally explodes, accompanied by a burst of shattered glass.

	It’s all so tediously predictable, shot with unsteady camera movements as if the tensions inside the sole location needed visual reinforcement. Because the plot required an outsider to expose more of the family’s history of dysfunctionality, an uninvited guest arrives in the form of Giulio (Tommaso Ragno), a writer who’ll be collaborating with Antonio on his next novel. An increasingly drunk Angela gets all flirty, alternating suggestive glances with a barrage of pointed insults designed to inflict maximum damage at everyone around her and then, with a plot twist that could be seen a mile off, new information arrives designed to elicit sympathy from this harridan’s children as well as the audience. La mamma è sempre la mamma.

	It’s a thankless role for Vanessa Scalera, pushed to extremes and forced to embody a woman whose one trait is bitterness; the script, based on a novel by Antonio Franchini, doesn’t even attempt to give her motivation. Angela takes up so much space there’s barely room for anything other than caricature, such as Paola’s laughable Buddhist husband Edoardo (Tony Laudadio), or Andrea, initially given some personality but then seen ludicrously performing ballet moves in the apartment — like Ann Miller in “The Man Who Came to Dinner,” only that film was a comedy.

	Perhaps some Italians will find Neapolitan Angela’s constant harping about Milan humorous, though far more amusing is how the film tries to pass off Antonio’s apartment as a Milan location, when everything about it (confirmed by the closing credits) says Naples. On top of it all, De Angelis (“The Vice of Hope”) decided the screaming matches needed a musical accompaniment of equal force. Between the noxious taunts, bubbling grease and cigarettes stubbed out in pasta, it’s enough to give anyone indigestion.

schema.headline: ‘The Fire Within You’ Review: An Insufferable Christmas Eve Family Drama in Which the Corrosive Rants Are as Noxious as the Dyspeptic Images

title: ‘Diarra From Detroit’ Creator Diarra Kilpatrick on the Season 2 Finale, Moving to Paramount+ and Why  Centering Black Women’s Stories Is ‘Inherently Political’
description:
SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from the Season 2 finale of “Diarra From Detroit” now streaming on Paramount+.

	With the P
body:
SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from the Season 2 finale of “Diarra From Detroit” now streaming on Paramount+.

	With the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger hanging in the balance and a presidential administration that is persistently hostile to diversity, Black-led series like Natasha Rothwell’s well-reviewed Hulu comedy “How to Die Alone,” Issa Rae’s HBO Max series, “Rap Sh*t” and even the NBC drama “Found” have all been given the ax. Black stories are rarely being greenlit on streamers and networks. Still, Paramount+’s “Diarra From Detroit,” a stellar blend of mystery, drama and romance, is shining high in its second season. Yet, the show’s endurance hasn’t been without its challenges. The series, which debuted in 2024 on BET+ to rave reviews, took a two-year hiatus before returning for its second season on Paramount+ this past July. (BET+ was shuttered last spring, with its programming being merged into Paramount+).​Created by star and executive producer Diarra Kilpatrick, this season, set amid a classic boiling-hot Detroit summer, finds Diarra trying to find her footing in her newfound relationship with Chris (Shannon Wallace), who is still reeling from his traumatic past. Without a summer school assignment, Diarra decides to use her free time to officially launch her P.I. business. However, being tasked with finding Chris’ uncle’s armoire (which actually turns out to be a desk) leads Diarra, Chris and the school teacher’s best friends Tea (Bryan Terell Clark) and Aja (Dominique Perry) into the underbelly of Detroit, chasing a treasure trove and evading some diabolical gangsters all while trying to iron out all of their personal drama and chaos in between.​“We love a gumbo; I love complexity,” Kilpatrick tells Variety. “It pisses me off when work that has a Black woman at the center of it doesn’t respect the audience. We’re not talking about good or bad. That’s a judgment that I’m not interested in. But do you respect the audience? Did you like this woman? I don’t want Black female work to be synonymous with low craftsmanship or low budgets or bad lighting. I want us to be honored. In the medium, in the space. It’s really dawning on me as people are asking me, how does it feel not to be a household name with a whole-ass show at a huge conglomerate where my show is being mentioned in the same breath as ‘Furious’ and ‘Lioness.’ Do you know how much those shows cost to produce? They have some of the biggest stars in the world in them. There was a moment when there was all this niche storytelling happening, and now I’m one of the last people standing.”​As “Diarra From Detroit” Season 2 comes to a close, Variety spoke with Kilpatrick about what it took to bring the second season to the small screen, why Black stories matter and her hopes for a possible Season 3.
	



	

									Paramount+
	


	
		Season 1 was very winter-coded. Did you always know that you wanted Season 2 to be set in the summer?	

	When we were shooting in the winter, I started thinking we should probably do a summer season. I think maybe John Chafin, who plays Danger, was like, “Can we move to the summer?” But that was always kind of the plan. I was hoping we would shoot in Detroit proper, and even as a Detroiter, I don’t really want to be in Detroit in the thick of winter. However, when I started writing the pilot, it was literally like the snow took over my body and wrote for me. I was like, “Snow is punishing the city streets.” I think the character was so sad and bereft [following her divorce from Swa, played by Morris Chestnut] that the weather forced itself into the story, externalizing her emotional place when she was really in the winter of her life. So I was very happy to go back to summer. I was also very happy when I saw the special effects budget for adding snow all the damn time. We had a budget cut, so summer felt much cheaper. No coats, no VFXing in snow. So there was that. But I do like the story to unfold in ways that feel like they make sense. I didn’t really know exactly where we would end up, but I knew we were going to come out of that season for her, and it felt fitting to do it in a literal sense as well.
	
	
		Speaking of budget cuts, is that part of the reason why it took so long between the first and second season?	

	It took them a very long time to pull the trigger on whether they were going to bring the show back. I imagine that had to do with whether they wanted to make the financial commitment. They decided that it would come back, but on a lower budget than Season 1. That impacted where we shot; we moved to Atlanta. It impacted a lot of things, cutting down some regular cast, that kind of thing. Part of it was just the corporate tango of nobody wanting to pull that trigger until the new regime was in place and had given the blessing to do so. We didn’t go into the [writers’] room for a really long time, and then they picked up the room. Then we went into the room, and the room ended, and they still hadn’t picked up the show. So then we were in limbo, waiting.
	
		In Season 2, “Diarra From Detroit” is still at its core an adventure and a mystery, but we also get a thread of romance. Diarra is being pulled between three men: Chris, Royce (Clifford “Method Man” Smith) and Danger. What was it like having a romantic element within the mystery-thriller adventure of it all, but also this thread of motherhood that Diarra is really pondering this entire time?	

	You really hit the nail on the head with the two things I love to play with in the show: the emotional truths of Black womanhood and the fantasy. We’re in a world now where it seems like nobody can agree on anything, but you know what we can agree on? Method Man is fine. John Chafin is fine. Morris Chestnut is still fine. So if we can’t come together over anything, let’s come together over that. Let’s give people a fantasy every week. I’ve said before, I’ll say it again, I love to see a Black woman at the center of a story, particularly one where she’s the object of desire. I think it’s healing not only for the audience, but it’s also expansive for everybody else to see that and to participate in Black womanhood and all of its glory. It’s a vibe. It’s a good time. Join the party. And I love that, because we hit so many emotional truths in the motherhood conversation; so many of my friends and I are struggling with that, talking about it or figuring it out. Because when we do that, it gives us the grace to go into some more far-fetched places, to go for some bigger laughs and bigger set pieces and to go into some of the fantasy, for the audience to go with us on the fantasy of being romanced by the finest of the fine, of wearing the best clothes, of running around solving a mystery in Detroit and still having your hair laid.
	



	

									BET/Paramount+
	


	
		You also weave this beautiful ribbon of history into the show. Audiences learn about bootlegging during Prohibition, the Underground Railroad and quilting and what that has meant for the Black community and the Black church specifically. Is “Diarra From Detroit” a political show? 	

	I would say anytime you put a Black woman in the center of something, it is inherently political in a lot of ways, simply because we just haven’t seen it enough for it to be old hat. People put so much on it. That’s where the fun is. Maybe I’m just a Black nerd, but I have always loved watching movies like “National Treasure” and “The Da Vinci Code.” I love watching a piece of fiction and then going on Google later to be like, “Wait a minute, how much of this is true and how much of these gaps are filled in by the imagination of the writer?” I guess at the end of the day, I’m the daughter of the teacher. So one thing [my mom] did was really instill in me the joy of learning, history and facts. “Indiana Jones,” “National Treasure” —  it’s like there are no Black women in these movies. At all. You struggle to find a Black woman who speaks; maybe she has two lines, rolls her neck and then moves on. I really wanted us to write in the very center of that genre. I think the facts give it legitimacy: it was well-researched and brought in some truths about the city. To me, we were kind of just following the genre playbook.
	
		Despite budget cuts and a change in platform, you also had so many people show up for you as guest stars this season, from Nicco Annan to Lovie Simone, Bokeem Woodbine, Lil Rel Howery, Amber Riley, Phylicia Rashad, Morris Chestnut and countless others. What has that meant for you?	

	As a community, Black Hollywood has a soul. Rel came into my DMs and was like, “I love this show.” When I hit him like, “We’re going to make you an offer,” he was down; he was in. Colman [Domingo] has said publicly that he would work for scale, which I keep repeating. That’s a big deal. It can be scary, because we operate a lot like an independent film. The way we shoot the show, no one gets all kinds of takes. You have to come in, do your thing, hit it and quit it. So there can be a fear in asking really prominent actors to come into a space where we’re going to be moving really quickly. But everybody came ready to play, loving the show, loving their character, and were just down to come in and sprinkle their magic over it. So it does make me emotional, because I was going a thousand miles per hour in the middle of it, just trying to get it done.
	
	
		Speaking of emotional, in the Season 2 finale, “A Cold Ass Wedding,” Diarra and Aja’s friendship breaks down. Why was that important to illustrate when their bond has been such a glue in the series?	

	I think Tea and Aja have been [Diarra’s] chosen family, and they’ve really been there for her even when her marriage was breaking down. But Diarra and Aja’s characters have been at real odds, and we’ve played it a lot for the comedy of it. Aja is the voice of reason, and Diarra pushes full throttle ahead. You can’t rob the audience of the inevitable, and it just felt like there was going to be an inevitable tension point between the two of them. Also, Dominique Perry is such a fantastic actress and so funny that I also wanted a chance to see her spread her dramatic wings a little bit there too. It felt inevitable that they’d reach a real impasse and that Aja would break. I don’t know that we know how to move through conflict as friends as well as we do in romantic relationships. So we just wanted to explore that, and we’ll see how their relationship is impacted, hopefully, if we get another season.



	

									Paramount+
	


	
		​Speaking of another season, what has it been like to experience the show on Paramount+, which is a much bigger platform than BET+ was?	

	It’s exciting, in a word — and it’s also complicated. BET+ going away meant a lot of people lost their jobs, and you can imagine that was a lot of Black people because it was at BET+. So you have to hope those people really land on their feet. But, as it relates to the show, I felt really excited about more people having access to this story. I really want to entertain a massive audience, and I want to bring them the nuance and specificity of me, Detroit, my sense of humor, my humanity and my heart. So it does feel like such an opportunity to reach a wider audience. The question is whether that audience will tap in, because I love that the Black audience has been really vocal on Threads, has made their opinions known, and has come to bully me to make sure that Diarra picks the man they like and all of that. But I have also seen people be like, “Wait, how come Paramount+ hasn’t shown me this show?” The algorithms are different, and we are in the echo chamber of our own algorithm, so it takes a little more time for other people to be introduced to the show and to tap in.
	

	
		What are your hopes about a potential Season 3?	

	Well, every season is a different mystery. Diarra will always have to deal with some consequences of the mess she stirred up, but I have some thoughts about what the new case would be, where they would go from here, and what the central mystery would be. 

	But the biggest mystery is her. She really struggles to investigate herself, even her own feelings. She loves distraction, like us all in this era of iPhones and whatever. It’s like the minute something uncomfortable happens, we’re all like, “Let me check my Instagram.” “TikTok time.” I think a lot of people will relate to that, but I do have some thoughts about what her next big internal question would be; we’ll have to see if we let any of that live. She also definitely answers the question Chris asked her at the very end.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: ‘Diarra From Detroit’ Creator Diarra Kilpatrick on the Season 2 Finale, Moving to Paramount+ and Why  Centering Black Women’s Stories Is ‘Inherently Political’

title: Chernin Entertainment Expands Film Team With Key Hire, Promotions (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Chernin Entertainment, the prolific independent film and TV producer founded by former News Corp. chairman Peter Chernin, has expanded its in-house
body:
Chernin Entertainment, the prolific independent film and TV producer founded by former News Corp. chairman Peter Chernin, has expanded its in-house film team.

	Under movies chief David Ready, the film unit has had big wins this year in theaters (“Backrooms”) and on streaming (Netflix’s “Apex”), and will continue to scale its slate.

	To fulfill that effort is new hire Marisa Paiva, who joins as an executive vice president of film. Paiva got her start Fox 2000 and spent over 13 years at the studio, working on literary adaptations like “Water for Elephants” and “Life of Pi.” She later oversaw the award-winning “Hidden Figures” and “The Woman in the Window.” She joined 3000 Pictures in 2019, developing “Lady Chatterley’s Lover” for Netflix and spearheading high-profile acquisitions like “Broken Country,” which Paiva will executive produce with Hello Sunshine.
	

	Paiva will join fellow EVP Brady Fujikawa, who joined the studio last year from Lionsgate. Fujikawa rises from his previous title of development and production lead. He oversaw the hot package “High Side,” which will put Timothée Chalamet in a motocross seat for director James Mangold. Fujikawa is also shepherding “Palm Grove,” starring Kate Hudson and Ana de Armas and directed by Kornél Mundruczó; and “One Month Mark,” a Jennifer Lawrence rom-com set up at Apple. He was previously at Good Universe (“Blockers,” “Good Boys”), and helped expand the John Wick universe at Lionsgate.


	Meanwhile, Samantha Nisenboim has been named senior vice president of film. Her producer credits include “The Lego Batman Movie,” The Tomorrow War” and “Renfield.” She is currently producing two feature films at Chernin, including the Netflix thriller “The Big Fix” starring Mark Wahlberg and Riz Ahmed. 
	

	Finally, Max Gains has been named creative executive. He began his career at Paramount before joining 21 Laps, where he spent six years working his way up from Shawn Levy’s assistant. His projects included “Deadpool & Wolverine,” “The Adam Project” and “Free Guy.”

	Ready told Variety that the company has “built a strong foundation and a slate we really believe in, and now we have the team to build out our next chapter. Marisa, Brady, Samantha, and Max are the kind of executives you want on your team – smart, relentless, deeply connected and driven by great material.”

	Chernin recently inked a new multi-year, first-look feature film deal with Apple Studios. In January, Mediawan announced an agreement to acquire Chernin parent The North Road Company. The combined entity will have major creative hubs across five continents and capabilities spanning all genres and formats.

schema.headline: Chernin Entertainment Expands Film Team With Key Hire, Promotions (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Has Already Made $50 Million in Pre-Sales, Three Months Before Release
description:
Doomsday typically indicates disaster, but for Marvel Studios that term is forecasting a booming box office.

	Disney reports that the next entry in
body:
Doomsday typically indicates disaster, but for Marvel Studios that term is forecasting a booming box office.

	Disney reports that the next entry in the sprawling Marvel Cinematic Universe, “Avengers: Doomsday,” has already made $50 million in domestic pre-sales, three months before the movie’s Dec. 18 release date. The studio reported that more than 70% of those pre-sales are for Infinity Vision tickets, emphasizing the audience’s appetite for premium large format screens. “Infinity Vision” is a new certification for premium large format theaters, which Disney unveiled at CinemaCon, touted as delivering “the biggest, brightest and most immersive cinematic experiences” for moviegoers.
	

	The pre-sale figures for “Doomsday” were announced Wednesday by Walt Disney Company senior executive VP & Chief Financial Officer, Hugh Johnston, at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference.


	Directed by Anthony and Joe Russo, the movie sees a massive assembly of Marvel superheroes, including the Avengers, Fantastic Four, Thunderbolts and the original X-Men, teaming up to face their most formidable foe yet: Victor Von Doom. Robert Downey Jr. returns to play the MCU’s new Big Bad after Tony Stark/Iron Man’s death at the end of “Avengers: Endgame.”

	In addition to Downey Jr. returning, Chris Evans is back as Steve Rogers/Captain America after he traveled back in time and stepped away from his superhero duties in “Endgame.” Chris Hemsworth also reprises his role as Thor, alongside Paul Rudd as Ant-Man, Letitia Wright as Black Panther, Sebastian Stan as the Winter Soldier, Tom Hiddleston as Loki and Simu Liu as Shang-Chi.
	

	“Doomsday” also marks the official MCU debut for several of Fox’s past “X-Men” stars after Disney acquired the studio. Patrick Stewart is back as Charles Xavier, Ian McKellen is Magneto, James Marsden is Cyclops, Kelsey Grammer is Beast, Rebecca Romijn is Mystique, Alan Cumming is Nightcrawler and Channing Tatum is Gambit.

	The “Fantastic Four: First Steps” stars, comprised of Pedro Pascal as Mister Fantastic, Vanessa Kirby as the Invisible Woman, Joseph Quinn as Human Torch and Ebon Moss-Bachrach as the Thing are back for “Doomsday,” as are the “Thunderbolts” cast, including Florence Pugh as Yelena Belova, David Harbour as Red Guardian, Lewis Pullman as Sentry, Wyatt Russell as U.S. Agent and Hannah John-Kamen as Ghost.

	Ahead of the film’s release, Marvel has also launched “Countdown to ‘Avengers: Doomsday‘ Official Podcast.” The podcast covers five films from the Infinity Saga: “The Avengers” (the subject of the podcast’s Aug. 27 debut episode); “Avengers: Age of Ultron” (Sept. 3); “Captain America: Civil War” (Sept. 10); “Avengers: Infinity War” (Sept. 17); and “Avengers: Endgame” (Sept. 24). All five films are available to stream on Disney+. The fifth episode of the podcast will coincide with the Sept. 25, 2026, re-release of “Avengers Endgame: Encore” in theaters.

title: Trump White House Pulls Down Tetris-Like Game, in Which You Had to Stop a ‘Zombie Siege’ at Mexican Border, After Company’s Copyright Threat
description: The White House has removed the “Build the Wall” game — a Tetris knockoff in which players were tasked with fortifying the southern U.S. border to k
body:
The White House has removed the “Build the Wall” game — a Tetris knockoff in which players were tasked with fortifying the southern U.S. border to keep out illegal immigrants — after the company that owns the rights to the popular title issued a statement saying it “take[s] copyright infringement very seriously.”

	Trump’s White House on Sept. 3 launched arcade.gov, featuring a collection of five MAGA-themed games. That included “Build the Wall” (with the subtitle “ZOMBIE BORDER SIEGE”). The foreign invaders from the Mexican side of the border bounced off the wall a player built and disintegrated, until the blocks were stacked above the upper bound and the game ended with the message “BORDER BREACHED.”
	

	As of Tuesday, the “Build the Wall” game was no longer available on the White House game site, as first spotted by gaming site Kotaku.


	Reps for the White House and the Tetris Company did not respond to requests for comment.

	Tetris Holding LLC is the owner of Tetris rights worldwide, and the Tetris Company is its exclusive licensee. In a statement posted to social media Friday, the Tetris Company said: “At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them. To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we’re grateful to have you in our community.”

	The company also noted it “was not involved in the creation of ‘Build the Wall.’” When asked whether the Tetris Company was considering taking legal action with respect to the White House’s game, a rep last Friday said the company was “reviewing the matter.” 
	

	Meanwhile, as of Wednesday afternoon, another anti-immigration game called “Rio Run,” which is patterned on the classic snake video-game genre, was still available on the White House game site. In that game, users “patrol the line” along the Rio Grande and collect illegal immigrants in a long chain behind a white officer in order to expel them from the U.S.

	The other games on the site are “Flappy Bill” (like “Flappy Bird”), in which users fly a bald eagle down the National Mall; “Trump Savings Tycoon,” where players use a net to catch bags of cash and other prizes to “Fill your kids’ Trump accounts”; and “Supply Line,” in which players sort food items on a school-lunch conveyer belt to “Make America Healthy Again.”

title: ‘Jupiter’ Review: A Claustrophobic Study of a Nuclear-Escalation Nightmare That Feels Too Small for the Big Screen
description: Fictional French President Paul Archambault, as played with gimlet-eyed resolve by Denis Menochet in Alexandre Smia‘s  “Jupiter” is, we’re cued to b
body:
Fictional French President Paul Archambault, as played with gimlet-eyed resolve by Denis Menochet in Alexandre Smia‘s  “Jupiter” is, we’re cued to believe, a good man. Thrust suddenly into a lurching nuclear crisis, he gathers ministers and advisers around him and listens intently to their staunchly opposing views on escalation vs appeasement. They are also good men and good women, cleaving to the same basic humanist principles, while disagreeing volubly on how to put them into practise. 
	

	Smia’s film takes a more solemn, less kinetic approach than Kathryn Bigelow’s similarly themed “A House Of Dynamite” but shares its tacit, strangely idealistic faith that the people tasked with thinking through the unthinkable in the event of a nuclear threat, will be dedicated public servants of intelligence and integrity. Given what we know of the world today, the movie’s bid for ruthless realism is slightly undercut by its desire to believe that those whose fingers hover reluctantly over the nuclear button have steady hands. 


	Then again it’s possible that brooding President Archambault only appears to be so selfless because the constricted screenplay (co-written by Smia and Thomas Finkielkraut though there scarcely seems room for two writers) doesn’t give him much self to speak of. As the film begins, Archambault, already ensnared in the tight close-up that DP Nicolas Loir’s relentlessly focussed, somber cinematography will rarely allow him to escape, is receiving some devastating news involving his daughter. It will later be mentioned a couple of times, but this thinly sketched personal tragedy is all the backstory we’ll ever get. Even Archambault’s own political affiliations are kept unspecified. 
	

	All we know for sure is that he is on friendly terms with the beleaguered Ukrainian president, Kovalenko. Ukraine is — if you can believe it — in need of military support due to ongoing attacks by Russia, whose premier, Chernov is — don’t know where they got this from — a volatile despot. When Chernov survives an assassination attempt, which was quite likely a false flag operation, he uses the pretext to ramp up the war, and Archambault must decide how far his pledge to protect Ukrainian sovereignty extends. At what point should a nuclear nation intervene, risking its own citizens’ safety, to defend an ally against the aggression of a powerful neighbor? His nominally sympathetic NATO allies refuse to commit to military intervention on the grounds that Ukraine is not a NATO member, so whatever France opts to do, she will be acting unilaterally. Then Chernov detonates an atomic bomb over the Black Sea as a show of force. Archambault and his advisers are moved to the bunker-like war room that gives the film its name. And the nuclear Doomsday clock ticks about twenty seconds closer to midnight. 

	There’s a prestige-TV-show feel to “Jupiter,” from its economical setting in the same few, featureless interior locations, to the division of the talky action into chapters with ominous headings like “Ultimatum” and “Sacrifice,” to the tension-building score from Olivier Marguerit, which is deployed lavishly over interstitial scenes of Archambault in the back of a car or striding purposefully down a passageway, the weight of the world on his bulky shoulders. The story moves swiftly, as cleanly edited by Pierre Deschamps, but it runs straight rather than deep. Even a fine supporting cast — including Reda Kateb as the hawkish Minister of Defence, Ella Rumpf as a diplomatic adviser and Céline Sallette as  French Prime Minister Clara Boyer — are treated more as mouthpieces for various points of view than as actual human beings. 

	And the insistent focus on Archambault to exclusion of all else does force Menochet’s sober gravitas to do a lot of the heavy lifting in terms of communicating the inner conflict and existential anguish with which all of the team must be struggling. When an aide reports that, with warheads armed and in the air, there are colleagues asking to be allowed take shelter in the bunker, Archambault tells him “Let in as many as you can.” But we never see that process occur, who gets let in and who is denied: as so often, Smia elects to turn away from a potentially emotive dilemma in the name of a paced-up procedural approach that makes “Jupiter” all pulse and no heart.  
	

	The situation escalates. The options narrow. After a few futile gambits, global geopolitics devolves from a game of chess to a game of chicken; the only strategy left is choosing whether to blink first without knowing if that blink will be interpreted as the compromise of the wise or the capitulation of the weak. Smia has made an impressively taut debut feature here, but it can feel controlled to a fault, with the iron grip on its grim tone paradoxically betraying a timidity when it comes to exploring the chaos and messiness of human behavior in the face of potential annihilation. As the film smash cuts to black on a frustratingly open-ended, very end-of-episode-one-style cliffhanger, the only conclusion is that in such a hellish scenario, no decision can ever be definitively judged to be the right one. So it’s hard not to feel a little unsatisfied at having just spent 87 minutes watching a man decide.

            Barry Melrose, the former NHL player, coach and longtime ESPN hockey analyst, has died ... his wife, Cindy, told ESPN.
      
    
            Melrose joined ESPN in 1996 and retired in 2023 after being diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He was best known for coaching Wayne Gretzky and the Los Angeles Kings to the 1993 Stanley Cup Final before becoming one of hockey’s most recognizable TV personalities.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            ESPN praised Melrose as a "distinctive and trusted" voice whose passion for the sport was unmistakable.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He was also known for his flashy suits, signature mullet and goatee ... and was beloved by colleagues and fans alike.
      
    
            Barry was 70.
      
    
            RIP.
